blocks.text: The day starts before the day

Ask Jensen Huang about work-life balance and he makes a joke of it. “I work as much as I can,” he told Stripe's Patrick Collison in 2024, while the room laughed. Then he explained that he works from the moment he wakes up to the moment he goes to bed, seven days a week. He sits through movies and cannot remember them, because he is thinking about work.

His wake-up time depends on when you ask. In 2023 he said ==5 a.m.==, with sleep by about 9:30 p.m. In 2024 he said six, because he feels guilty waking his dogs, so he lies still and reads in bed until then. The Financial Times had reported a 4 a.m. start in 2020, for exercise and family time, and on Joe Rogan's podcast in late 2025 he talked about checking email from 4 a.m.
Every day. Every single day. Not one day missed. Including Thanksgiving, Christmas.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang on The Joe Rogan Experience, as reported by Fortune, December 2025

blocks.text: The trick that matters is the order, not the hours. At Caltech in 2024 he described his morning: he keeps a clear priority list and starts with the top item before he even reaches the office. __By the time his workday begins, the most important job is already finished.__ So when people apologise for interrupting him, he can honestly tell them he has plenty of time. His biographer Stephen Witt names the same habit as one of his two main scheduling tricks.
Copy this one tomorrow morning. Hardest task first, before your phone wins.
Only problem meetings allowed

Huang says he hates reporting meetings. People do not have to report to him, he told Collison. He goes to problem meetings, idea meetings and brainstorming meetings, and leaves regular operations to the people who run them. He also says he tries hard not to let Outlook manage his life.
CEOs are pinch hitters. We should be working on the things that nobody else can or nobody else is.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, Stripe Sessions, 2024

blocks.text: His meetings look different too. Bloomberg reported that he has no time for detailed PowerPoint decks. A write-up on Tae Kim's Substack says Nvidia uses whiteboards in meetings instead, and that people still remember one meeting where Huang listened to someone else present for a full hour, because it was so unusual. A 2023 Times of India summary of his leadership interview said Nvidia also skips the five-year and one-year plans most big companies use, and keeps adjusting to the market instead.
Sixty direct reports

Most CEOs run a small circle of five to ten executives. Huang has more than ==60== people reporting straight to him. His logic is simple: the people at the top need the least managing, so the CEO should have the most reports. He told Collison that this removes something like seven layers from the company.

He also refuses to hold private meetings with them. “I don't do one-on-ones,” he said at Stripe. His staff meets about once every two weeks, around whatever problems exist, and everyone hears the same reasoning at the same moment. In 2026 he told Lex Fridman the reason in fewer words: “I don't have one-on-ones with them because it's impossible.”
There's not one piece of information that I somehow secretly tell the staff; I don't tell the rest of the company.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang at Stanford, reported by Fortune, June 2024

items.label: Layers of management he says this removes
Top-5 emails he scans each morning, per the WSJ
Nvidia staff turnover in its 2024 report, against 17.7% for the chip industry

blocks.text: He does not call it a rule for everyone. When Collison asked whether each of the 60 also gets 60 reports, Huang said no, because people lower down need more supervision. The structure can still spread in messy ways: one former support worker told Bloomberg his supervisor had more than 100 direct reports. And Huang says that if someone truly needs him privately, he will drop everything for them.
Sixty sounds crazy. He says it isn't scalable down the ladder. Don't copy blindly.
Five bullets that reach the top

Nvidia staff send short notes called T5Ts, or Top-5 Things: what they are working on, what they are thinking about, what they have noticed. The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang looks at about 100 of them every morning, then reads more on Sunday nights with a glass of his favourite Scotch. “If you send it, I'll read it,” he says. Reporter Tae Kim explains why: in most companies a status report gets cleaned up at every layer, until the CEO receives something with the bad news removed.
I'm looking to detect the weak signals. It's easy to pick up the strong signals, but I want to intercept them when they are weak.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang to Tae Kim, reported by Fortune, January 2025

blocks.text: The Journal credits these emails with helping him decide, years ago, that Nvidia needed to boost workloads on its graphics chips. He does not send a T5T of his own, because he fears everyone else's would start to copy it. “I have my own Top-5 Things that I keep to myself,” he said. As Nvidia grew, even this system had to change: in January 2026 its big field sales group narrowed distribution to a much smaller group that still includes Huang.

For example: because Huang often answers within minutes, staff learned to time their emails. Don't send it late on a Friday evening, one former employee told Kim. “It would wreck your weekend.” Most people send theirs late on Sunday instead, just as he settles down with his single malt, so they can act on his reply when the week starts.

Email is his main voice. The New Yorker reported that he writes hundreds a day, often only a few words long. One executive compared them to haiku, and another to ransom notes. On Rogan's show he estimated that he reads several thousand emails a day, and Kim says people who left Nvidia 20 years ago can still get a reply within a minute.
Haiku or ransom notes. Either way: short, clear, no place to hide.
How he decides

He has catchphrases, and they are working tools. “The speed of light” means asking how fast a task could possibly be done, then working backwards to a real deadline. The “zero-billion-dollar market” means a product with no rivals and no obvious customers yet. Nvidia also has a defining mantra, reported by Business Insider from Kim's book: “The mission is the boss.” A project leader can suddenly find themselves reporting directly to Huang as a “pilot in charge”.

For example: when Nvidia's headquarters was being designed, a virtual-reality headset took five hours to show a design change. Under Huang's pushing, engineers got it down to ten seconds. The lead architect, Hao Ko, later explained why that was not just bullying. At five hours he would have settled for any adequate shade of green, and at ten seconds he could pick the best one.

When he changes direction, it can happen in a weekend. Nvidia vice-president Greg Estes told the New Yorker about the moment Huang bet the company on neural networks. In Estes's telling, an email went out on a Friday evening saying everything was going to deep learning and that Nvidia was no longer a graphics company. Bryan Catanzaro, then Nvidia's lead deep-learning researcher, admitted he had doubts about the bet, and later admitted Huang was right.
By Monday morning, we were an A.I. company. Literally, it was that fast.
blocks.who: Greg Estes, Nvidia vice-president, to The New Yorker, 2023

blocks.text: So does he delegate? Yes and no. Staff have real freedom, and Nvidia was still remote-friendly in 2025. But Bloomberg reported that he will step into small choices, such as which photo to use in a marketing campaign. Fortune's 2024 profile quoted Arm's Rene Haas describing him as “reaching down into different layers of the organization”, and Fortune added its own blunter word: micromanaging. A former director told Business Insider: “His ability to track small details across countless projects is incredible.”
Hiring, firing and “torture”

Collison once heard Huang say he rarely fires people, and asked about it on stage. Huang's answer started with his own life. “I used to clean bathrooms, and now I'm the CEO of a company,” he said, so he believes most jobs can be learned. He then said, tongue in cheek, that he would rather push people until they got it.
So I'd rather torture you into greatness because I believe in you.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, Stripe Sessions, 2024

blocks.text: He hires fast, but with a limit. At a November 2025 all-hands he said Nvidia had hired several thousand people in one quarter and was still about 10,000 short, but that hiring should match how quickly new people can be integrated. In that same meeting he heard that some managers were telling staff to use less AI. “Are you insane?” he replied, and added: “I promise you, you will have work to do.”

Money helps hold people in place. Staff can put up to 15% of their salary into Nvidia shares at a 15% discount, and stock grants usually vest over four years. Former employees described this to Bloomberg as golden handcuffs. In January 2026 Huang said Nvidia had about 40,000 people, and that many stay for 20 to 25 years.
What it is like to work for him

The people who worked there in the early days describe a place that never stopped. Former CFO Geoff Ribar sat near Huang and learned that the first person he saw each morning got “the first blast”, whatever the topic. Ribar used to tell rivals to count the cars in Nvidia's parking lot on weekends. Marketing director Andrew Logan left one night to take his wife to a 9:30 p.m. showing of Titanic, and a coworker shouted, “Oh, half day, Andy?”

For example: engineer Kenneth Hurley was at a urinal when Huang stepped up beside him and asked, “Hey, what's up?” Hurley said “not much”, got a sideways look, and panicked. So he listed twenty things he was working on. “Okay,” said Huang.
No place in that building was safe. Not even that one.

The recent accounts are harder. Ten current and former staff spoke to Bloomberg in 2024, all anonymously. One described seven-day weeks ending at 1 or 2 a.m. Another described seven to ten meetings a day, each with more than 30 people, often with fighting and shouting. She warned that the flat structure can push people to compete for Huang's attention rather than work together.

Huang's public criticism is real, and it is deliberate. The Telegraph's review of Witt's book opens with a chip architect being berated in front of about 150 colleagues for an hour and a half or more, an experience staff call “the Wrath of Huang”. The company's former chief scientist explained the logic: “He would never just yell at some guy in the hall.” Huang's own version is calmer. “I give you feedback right there in front of everybody,” he told Collison, because everyone should learn from it, and he adds that half the time he is the one who is wrong.
I've been afraid of Jensen sometimes, but I also know that he loves me.
blocks.who: Bryan Catanzaro, Nvidia researcher, to The New Yorker, 2023

blocks.text: That quote is the whole puzzle in one line. Catanzaro left Nvidia for another company and came back. Jeff Fisher, an original employee, is now very wealthy and still works: “Many of us are financial volunteers at this point.” Witt says some staff think the anger is deliberate theatre and trade custom Jensen emojis, and one review of his book notes that Huang could be very generous to staff facing medical problems. Glassdoor reviewers gave him 97% approval, according to Bloomberg, as reported by Mint.

Told on 60 Minutes that people call him demanding, a perfectionist and not easy to work for, he agreed. “It should be like that,” he said. “If you want to do extraordinary things, it shouldn't be easy.” His own explanation of the temper is odd and rather honest: “It's really about what's going on in my brain versus what's coming out of my mouth. When the mismatch is great, then it comes out as anger.” __Remember that all of this was built by a founder with decades of context, and for him.__
I built Nvidia in a way where I could drive it, and manage it, and steer it perfectly.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, quoted on Tae Kim's Key Context, 2026

blocks.text: Belief 1: Suffering builds the thing that matters

In March 2024 Huang stood in front of Stanford students, some of the most credentialed young people in America, and wished them misery. He said his great advantage was very low expectations. People with very high expectations, he argued, have very low resilience, because they have never been ready for failure. It sounded like a joke, and he was completely serious.
Greatness is not intelligence. Greatness comes from character. And character isn't formed out of smart people, it's formed out of people who suffered.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang at Stanford, reported by CNBC, March 2024

blocks.text: This comes from his own life: the Kentucky school, the bathrooms, the near-death of his company. He does not pretend suffering is fun. “I don't love every day of my job,” he told Collison. “I don't think every day brings me joy nor does joy have to be the definition of a good day.” At Caltech he listed his superpowers, and intelligence was not at the top. Enduring pain and working on one thing for a very long time were.

Here is the twist young founders should hear. Asked in 2023 what company he would start if he were 30 again, he said, “I wouldn't do it.” Building Nvidia, he said, was ==a million times harder== than anyone expected, with vulnerability, embarrassment and shame he would not choose to repeat. __He says he still tricks his brain by asking, “How hard can it be?”__ In his view, the entrepreneur's superpower is not knowing the answer.
A trillion-dollar founder says nobody in their right mind would start. Read twice.
Belief 2: You are always about to die

When Nvidia's RIVA 128 chip reached stores, the company had enough money for one month of payroll. Huang never let that feeling go. For years he opened staff presentations with the words “Our company is thirty days from going out of business.” Tae Kim's book admits this was hyperbole on one level, and says it also tested new hires: if they could not take the pressure, they should leave early.

For example: long-time Nvidia manager Dwight Diercks remembers that it always felt like the company was at zero. However much money sat in the bank, Huang could explain how three things could happen and all of it would be gone. Veteran Jeff Fisher says the fear clears your head, because you are always trying to see around corners.

Thirty-three years later, running the most valuable company on earth, he told Rogan the feeling had not changed. He called it exhausting and said he is always in a state of anxiety. Asked what drives him, he gave an unusual answer. At a 2023 New York Times event he had said it another way: “I don't wake up proud and confident. I wake up worried and concerned.”
I have a greater drive from not wanting to fail than the drive of wanting to succeed.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang on The Joe Rogan Experience, December 2025

blocks.text: Belief 3: Say the embarrassing thing early

In the mid-1990s Nvidia had one big contract, to build a chip for a Sega game console. A year in, Huang realised the whole approach was wrong. If he finished the job, Nvidia would own inferior technology. If he did not, it would run out of money. So he contacted Sega's chief executive, Shoichiro Irimajiri, told him to find another partner, and then asked to be paid in full anyway.

“I was embarrassed to ask,” Huang told graduates in Taipei in 2023. Irimajiri agreed, and Huang said the deal “gave us six months to live.” On Rogan's show he added a detail: the remaining $5 million was turned into an investment. __Most founders hide this kind of problem until it kills them.__ Huang went to the one person who could end the company and told him the truth.
Confronting our mistake and, with humility, asking for help saved NVIDIA.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, National Taiwan University commencement, May 2023

blocks.text: Very important for first-time founders! Bad news doesn't get cheaper with time.
Belief 4: Build for customers who don't exist yet

In 2007 Nvidia put CUDA, its software system for general computing, into all its graphics chips. It was expensive and paid little for years. “Our market cap hovered just above a billion dollars,” Huang recalled. “Our shareholders were skeptical of CUDA and preferred we improve profitability.” The New Yorker compared him to the farmer in Field of Dreams, who builds a baseball diamond in a cornfield and waits for players to come.

He does not call this gambling. The New Yorker describes a practical man who has never read a science-fiction novel and dislikes speculation. He reasons from what chips can do today, then bets heavily on what they will do next. At Stanford he said he keeps sending the company back to first principles, asking how he would build a computer from scratch given today's tools. His 2024 advice to Caltech graduates follows from this: believe in something unexplored, but let it be informed and reasoned.
Belief 5: Knowing what to give up is the real skill

In 2010 Nvidia charged into mobile phone chips. By his telling it did well at first, then modem makers learned to build computing chips faster than Nvidia learned to build modems. He could have fought for a share of a huge market. He left instead, and told the Taipei graduates that the retreat freed Nvidia to build computers for robots and cars, a market worth zero billion dollars at the time. Deciding what to give up, he said, is at the very core of success.
By leaving the phone market, we opened our minds to invent a new one.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, National Taiwan University commencement, May 2023

blocks.text: Quitting isn't failing if you know exactly what you're quitting for.
Belief 6: No job is beneath you

At Stanford's business school in 2024, he was asked why he designed such a flat company. He did not begin with management theory. He began with toilets. He then explained what that attitude looks like at the top: if someone sends him their work and wants his input, he will go through it and show how he reasons about it, and he says he learns from it as well.
To me, no task is beneath me because, remember, I used to be a dishwasher, and I mean that. I used to clean toilets.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, Stanford Graduate School of Business, 2024

blocks.text: Belief 7: Hoarded information is fake power

Huang thinks most corporate hierarchies exist to protect secrets. He mocks the idea that a CEO's knowledge is so precious it can be shared with only two or three people. His job, he says, is to create the conditions for people to do their life's work, and they can only act well if they understand the situation, even when it is hard to hear. He has a memorable phrase for what layers of managers do to the truth: “information mutilation”.
I don't believe in a culture, in an environment where the information that you possess is the reason why you have power.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, Stanford Graduate School of Business, 2024

blocks.text: Belief 8: Find a craft, and you have plenty of time

The most gentle story he tells comes from a family summer in Japan. On a suffocating day in Kyoto, at the Silver Temple, he noticed one gardener squatting in a huge moss garden, picking at the moss with bamboo tweezers and dropping it into a basket that looked empty. Huang walked over and asked what he was doing. The man said he was picking dead moss and taking care of his garden. Huang pointed out that the garden was very big.
I have cared for my garden for 25 years. I have plenty of time.
blocks.who: A gardener in Kyoto, as retold by Jensen Huang at Caltech, 2024

blocks.text: Huang called it one of the most profound lessons of his life. It ties together two sides of him that look contradictory. In Taipei he told graduates to run, “either you are running for food; or you are running from becoming food.” In Pasadena he told graduates to find a craft and let it be their life's work. __Running hard and having plenty of time are the same idea when you have chosen one thing.__
He has run the same company for over thirty years. Plenty of time.

chapters.title: Family, Dogs and a Quiet Fortune

blocks.text: The people at home

Huang and Lori Mills married after Oregon State, and both worked in Silicon Valley as chip designers. “She actually made more than me,” he told the New Yorker. Within a few years she left the workforce to raise their children while he ran a division and studied at Stanford at night. Her name is on the family's foundation as president.

He is not shy about what that support meant. When the Acquired hosts asked how anyone survives the emotional damage of building a company, he named family, friends and colleagues who never gave up on him. Witt, who spent years studying him, describes a goofy dad at home who likes to cook and throw a baseball around. Beyond that he says little, and The Atlantic's review of Witt's book notes his reluctance to talk about himself.
You need the unwavering support of people around you.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, Acquired podcast, October 2023

blocks.text: Their two children, Spencer and Madison, are adults, and their careers have been widely reported. In 2017 Fortune described them as a speakeasy owner and a hospitality professional. Madison trained in cooking, and Spencer ran a cocktail bar in Taipei. Then both moved to Nvidia, Madison in 2020 and Spencer in 2022, working on simulation software and robotics. The New Yorker's dry phrase for how this happened was “following years of paternal browbeating”.

Huang's parents are still part of the story too. In 2024 he said they “work hard today”, and in 2023 they sat in the audience in Taipei when he gave the speech at National Taiwan University. On Rogan's show he said both his kids work at Nvidia and work every day. Whether you read that as sweet or alarming probably says something about you.
His kids work every day too. Decide if that's your goal.
Sleep, anxiety and the off switch

We found no public report of a major health crisis, so we will not guess at one. What he has spoken about openly is the mental load. He told Rogan the job is exhausting and that he is always in a state of anxiety. When the New Yorker asked about the bullying he faced as a boy, he said there was no counsellor back then, and you simply had to toughen up and move on. His biographer says he hates losing so much that he still seemed upset about a high-school table tennis final.

Sleep is where his answers change the most. In 2023 he told Norway's wealth fund chief, “I like my sleep and sleep is really important to me.” In October 2026, asked about bringing data centres online faster, he offered a different mantra: “Try less sleep, which is what I do.” He also claims that work itself calms him. “Working is relaxing for me,” he said, adding that the most relaxing thing of all is hanging out with his family.
Don't copy the sleep part. Your brain is your only factory.
How he spends

He does not live like a monk. He flies by private jet, and the embossed Tom Ford biker jacket he wore in Taiwan in 2024 cost about $9,000. But he also goes back to Denny's. Over one breakfast there with the New Yorker's reporter he ordered seven items, rolled a pancake around a sausage with his fingers, and then tipped the waitress a thousand dollars. His 2026 pay package was $36.3 million, which is small next to his shares: Nvidia's latest proxy lists him with 3.58% of the company.

items.label: His fiscal 2026 pay, down 27% on smaller stock awards
Nvidia stock listed against his name in the 2026 proxy
Net assets of the Huangs' foundation, end of 2024
The tip he left at Denny's

blocks.text: A giant, silent foundation

Jensen and Lori started their foundation in 2007 with 370,000 Nvidia shares worth ==$12.6 million==. Those shares did what Nvidia shares did. By the end of 2024 the foundation held about $9.1 billion in net assets, one of the 15 largest private foundations in the US according to the data firm FoundationMark. Lori is listed as president and Jensen as secretary and CFO, both on zero pay.

What it actually does is harder to see. As of 2023 it had no paid staff, and it has no website. For its first nine years it never made more than one grant a year. Most of its money goes to donor-advised funds, accounts where a donor gets a tax deduction now and can decide later where the money goes, with no deadline and no public list of recipients. In 2023 one such fund received $46 million, which was 77% of the foundation's giving.

The public gifts lean towards education and their own history. They pledged $50 million towards a $213 million research complex at Oregon State that carries both their names. In 2019 he gave a building to the Kentucky school where he once cleaned the bathrooms. In 2025 they gave $22.5 million to the California College of the Arts. Private foundations must by law pay out about 5% of assets a year, so as the fortune grows the giving should grow too, and FoundationMark estimated $369 million would be due for 2025.
Giving at this scale is a skill too. Watch what he does next.
Taxes

In December 2024 the New York Times reported, from securities and tax filings, that Huang had used popular loopholes in the federal estate and gift taxes. The paper estimated the savings for his family at roughly ==$8 billion==. The report described moves that use gaps in the law, not a criminal case. A year later California campaigners proposed a one-time 5% tax on billionaires' wealth, which might cost him nearly $8 billion. Other tech executives criticised it and threatened to leave the state.
We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang on Bloomberg Television, reported by CNBC, January 2026

chapters.title: The Rock Star Who Hates the Stage

blocks.text: Here is the strangest fact about the most watched CEO in technology: he says he hates this part. “I hate public speaking,” he told the New Yorker's reporter while nervously rocking on his feet before a talk. When more than 11,000 people screamed for him at Nvidia's 2024 conference, he told 60 Minutes it was the scariest he had ever been. “I'm an engineer. I'm not a performer.”

Witt, who knows him as well as any outsider, says the nerves are real, even after thousands of talks. On The Times's tech podcast, in an episode built around an interview with Witt, the public Jensen is called an act, a carefully cultivated persona. Both can be true. __A brand can be a costume you choose on purpose, as long as the work underneath is real.__
If you get nervous before speaking, good. So does he.
The jacket, the tattoo, the kitchen

An Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC he has worn a leather jacket for more than two decades, and he credits his wife and daughter for the look. He has kept it on even in humid Singapore. Before one event in 2023, he spent six minutes mocking Nvidia's architect for wearing the same outfit with too many pockets. “Simplify, man!” he said. Mark Zuckerberg swapped jackets with him in 2024, and called him “Taylor Swift, but for tech”.

The tattoo story is pure comedy. At a company off-site someone asked what the team would do if the stock hit $100. People offered a shaved head, blue hair and a nipple ring, and by the time it reached Huang the bidding had reached tattoo level. The stock hit $100, and he got the Nvidia logo on his shoulder.
I was crying like a baby. My kids were with me, and they're like, 'Dad, you've gotta control yourself.'
blocks.who: Jensen Huang to Fortune, 2017

blocks.text: Six years later a host asked what was next. “Ageing gracefully. No more tattoos,” he said. “It hurts way more than anybody tells you.” During the pandemic he invented another signature: his kitchen. In one launch video he reached for a pot holder and lifted a chip the size of a baking sheet from his oven, telling viewers it had been cooking for a while.

For example: in August 2021 Nvidia revealed a trick from its April keynote. Engineers had scanned his face and body, trained an AI to mimic his gestures, and built a perfect digital copy of his kitchen. For 14 seconds of a presentation lasting 1 hour 48 minutes, the man on screen was not him. Nvidia said the stunt left its audience wondering how much of the keynote was real, and that was exactly the point of the demo.
How he talks

His style is a running deadpan with a serious point inside. Worried that AI might replace humans the way cars replaced horses? “Horses have limited career options,” he told the New Yorker. “For example, horses can't type.” He tells the dishwasher story everywhere, because it works. “There's no magic,” he told 60 Minutes. “It's just 61 years of hard work every single day.”

His media habits are unusual for a modern billionaire. Nvidia's official X account has carried statements from him, but he built his fame mostly through long keynotes and long-form conversations. In recent years he has done Acquired, 60 Minutes, Joe Rogan and Lex Fridman. Those shows suit him because they give him time to tell the whole story. He is much less keen on people probing his inner life, and The Atlantic notes that his reluctance to talk about himself made him a challenging subject for Witt.
Jensanity: how the world sees him

In Taiwan he is treated like a pop star. Local media call it “Jensanity”. During the 2024 Computex fair, TV crews followed him everywhere, and restaurants he ate at saw business boom. He threw the first pitch at a baseball game and walked a night market. At one point he signed a woman's top and wondered aloud whether this was a good idea. Colleagues and other chip executives were bemused, and some noted that this kind of attention never happens in the US.
He's like a pop star. That's how we view him.
blocks.who: Amanda Shih, a finance worker at Computex in Taipei, to Reuters, 2024

blocks.text: A chip designer mobbed for selfies. Twenty years ago this was impossible.

South Korea got its own moment in October 2025. On his first official visit in more than a decade, he went to a local fried-chicken restaurant called Kkanbu with Samsung's Jay Y. Lee and Hyundai's Chung Euisun. Photos of the three men with beer and chicken went viral, and Bloomberg reported that investors drove up Korean fried-chicken stocks. China is more complicated. He went there three times in 2025 in what Reuters called a charm offensive, and said about half the world's AI researchers are Chinese, while his company was squeezed by both governments.
India: a promise and a missed date

India matters to him, and he says so in his own stories. He recalls that about six years before 2024, Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked him to address the Indian cabinet on artificial intelligence. “It was literally the first time any government leader, any national leader asked me to address his cabinet on this particular topic,” he said. In his retelling, Modi later gave him a line about value: India should not just export flour to import bread.

He carried that line onto a Mumbai stage on 24 October 2024, at Nvidia's AI Summit, sitting beside Mukesh Ambani of Reliance. “You should not export data to import intelligence,” he said, and the two men talked through how Reliance and Nvidia would build AI infrastructure in India. Then in February 2026 he was expected to be one of the biggest names at the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi. He withdrew days before, with Nvidia citing “unforeseen circumstances” and sending executive Jay Puri to lead a senior delegation.
It makes complete sense that India should manufacture its own AI.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, Nvidia AI Summit, Mumbai, October 2024

blocks.text: Indian readers see two Jensens in their own papers. One is the immigrant dishwasher who was invited to address India's cabinet. The other appears in headlines about workers paying with 2 a.m. workdays, and in stories about a boss who says he works from the moment he wakes until bedtime. Young Indian founders should notice that the second is the price of the first, and decide for themselves how much of it they want.
Close to power

In Washington his image is built on access. He told Rogan that when he first spoke to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Lutnick called him and Nvidia a national treasure and said he could call any time. “Every single time I called, if I needed something, I want to get something off my chest, express some concern, they're always available,” he said. The San Francisco Standard reported that he heaped praise on President Trump, and that he had helped talk him out of sending the National Guard to San Francisco. To admirers this is statesmanship, and to critics it is a chip seller lobbying for his own sales, a tension the next chapter returns to.

Huang tells some of his failures beautifully on stage. Others he tells less often, and a few ended in court papers. This chapter lists them plainly. Where a case is still open we say so, because an accusation is not a verdict.
The early technology bet

Nvidia's first chips used quadrilaterals to draw 3D shapes while rivals used triangles. Then Microsoft announced that its graphics software would support only triangles. Huang's own verdict at Taipei was that the approach was technically poor. In 1996 he laid off more than half of about 100 staff and bet what was left on untested chips. “It was fifty-fifty,” he said, “but we were going out of business anyway.”
He was thirty-three and sacking half his staff. Check the industry standard first.
2008: the laptops that wouldn't start

In July 2008 Nvidia disclosed that some of its laptop graphics chips were failing at unusually high rates, because of weak materials. Screens went blank or scrambled. HP named 24 affected models and Dell 15, and both made fans run harder to hold off the failures. Nvidia booked a ==$196 million== charge, nearly eight times its normal warranty reserve across all its products.

The way it was handled hurt too. Huang stressed that Nvidia was not obliged to replace the chips. Apple later said that, contrary to what it had been told by Nvidia months earlier, some MacBook Pros did contain the flawed parts. A class action followed and was settled: owners could get replacement parts, a replacement computer or reimbursement. An appeals court upheld the deal in 2013, including $13 million in lawyers' fees, noting that about 5 million consumers had been notified.
The phone years

The strategic retreat from phones makes a lovely speech, and we told it that way earlier. The balance sheet version is rougher. In 2011 Nvidia paid $367 million for Icera, a modem company, to get into smartphones. Ars Technica called Nvidia something of a non-entity in phones, and the Icera-equipped chip landed in only a handful of devices. In 2015 Nvidia wound Icera down, in a unit of about 500 people. It can be true that leaving was wise and that going in was costly.
A brave exit and an expensive entry. Both are true.
Rough edges with customers and partners

Two smaller episodes show how a dominant company can look from the outside. In 2016 Nvidia agreed to settle consumer suits claiming it misled buyers about a graphics card's performance and storage, paying $30 per buyer plus $1.3 million in lawyers' fees. In March 2018 it launched the GeForce Partner Program, which The Verge said amounted to pressing card makers to tie their gaming brands exclusively to Nvidia. After two months of anger Nvidia cancelled it, while complaining of “rumors, conjecture, and mistruths” and denying it had wanted exclusivity.
The crypto problem

This one reached the US Supreme Court, and Huang personally was named. In 2017 and 2018, crypto miners bought huge numbers of Nvidia gaming chips. The SEC later found Nvidia failed to disclose in two quarterly reports that crypto mining was a significant driver of its gaming revenue growth. In 2022 Nvidia paid a ==$5.5 million== penalty, without admitting or denying the findings. Inside the company, Witt reports, many engineers considered crypto an idiotic distraction.

Investors sued separately. They point to Huang saying “Crypto is small for us” and “Our core business is elsewhere.” In November 2018 Nvidia missed its revenue target by 2% amid a sharp crypto falloff, and the stock fell 28.5% over two sessions. Nvidia has always denied wrongdoing and has fought every step. As the case stands, no court has found that it or Huang committed fraud. Reuters noted the odd backdrop: anyone who bought in 2017 and held on has since gained 3,400% or more.

items.text: Shareholders sue Nvidia and executives including Huang.
A federal judge dismisses the case.
The Ninth Circuit partly revives it, keeping claims against Huang and Nvidia.
The Supreme Court hears Nvidia's appeal, then dismisses it as improvidently granted.
The judge certifies an investor class. Nvidia asks the Ninth Circuit to step in.
Investors tell the judge they have struck a deal with Nvidia. We could not confirm the terms.

blocks.text: Be loud about risky revenue. The $5.5M fine was the cheap part.
Arm: the $40 billion deal that died

In September 2020 Huang agreed to buy Arm, whose designs run nearly every smartphone, from SoftBank. The price was then valued at $40 billion. Customers including Microsoft, Qualcomm and Google worried Nvidia would restrict access. The US Federal Trade Commission sued to block it in December 2021, and British regulators raised national security concerns. In February 2022 the deal was abandoned.

The bill was real. SoftBank kept Nvidia's $1.25 billion prepayment, and Nvidia took a ==$1.36 billion== charge. Nvidia did keep a 20-year Arm licence, which it now uses for its own processors, so the loss had a silver lining. “We gave it our best shot,” Huang told analysts. The miss was believing that being the best at something would convince everyone who depended on Arm to trust you with it.

items.label: Charge from the dead Arm deal, 2022
Charge from the H20 China ban, 2025

blocks.text: China: caught between two governments

No business problem has cost him more attention. US export limits blocked Nvidia's best chips from China. In 2025 new US limits on the H20, a chip Nvidia had designed for China, led to a $4.5 billion charge. “We went from 95% market share to 0%,” Huang said in October 2025, calling the policy a mistake.

Nvidia then agreed to give the US government 15% of certain China sales, an unusual arrangement. Chinese officials, meanwhile, summoned Nvidia about alleged backdoors, which it denies, and in September 2025 China's regulator said a preliminary probe found Nvidia broke antitrust law over its 2020 Mellanox purchase. Nvidia says it complies with the law in all respects, and the regulator said it would keep investigating.

Even the win arrived late. President Trump cleared the H200 chip in December 2025 in exchange for a 25% cut. In May 2026 Reuters reported that about 10 Chinese firms were approved with no deliveries yet. Tom's Hardware reported the first deliveries in August: roughly 10,000 chips each to ByteDance and Tencent. Nvidia's forecast that same month assumed no data-centre compute revenue from China at all.

His words made it worse at times. In November 2025 he told the Financial Times, “China is going to win the AI race.” Within hours Nvidia posted a softer line on X: “China is nanoseconds behind America in AI.” Critics in Washington accused him of putting sales first. A sharp opinion piece in Foreign Policy said Nvidia's private interests had beaten national security when a chip-export bill was left out of a defence law. Huang argues that keeping the world's developers on American chips is how America wins. That argument remains unsettled, and it happens to match his revenue.
One line to a newspaper, then hours of cleaning up. Watch your words.
AI's open questions

Three newer fights are unresolved, so read these carefully. Authors say Nvidia trained AI models on pirated books; in May 2026 a federal judge let direct and contributory claims go forward and dismissed a vicarious claim, which is an early step and not a finding of copying. In September 2026, Reuters and Bloomberg reported that the Justice Department was examining whether Nvidia structured its late-2025 licensing deal with chip startup Groq to avoid antitrust review. Nvidia called the deal a prime example of the American system working as designed.

The third is money going around in circles. In September 2025 Nvidia said it planned to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI, a big customer. By February 2026 Huang was saying, “It was never a commitment,” and Nvidia settled on $30 billion. It has also backed partners' data centres, including a guarantee of up to $105 billion on one OpenAI project in Ohio. Critics say this blurs the line between real demand and vendor financing. Huang stays confident, and in October 2026 he said demand from these cloud companies was “off the charts”, even as their shares fell at least 30% that month.
If your customer's money is your money, count your sales twice.
The temper and the empty chair

The last two costs are personal. Witt's book ends with Huang yelling at him when he raised the risks of AI. Business Insider's headline summed it up: he shot down comparisons to Elon Musk and yelled at his biographer. He told Witt he was a serious person doing serious work. The New Yorker had noted earlier that he did not sign the 2023 statement comparing AI risk to nuclear war, and said he had never worried about the technology, not once. A leader who shouts down a hard question teaches his whole staff not to ask it.

The other cost is succession. Nvidia has no publicly disclosed successor plan, and the company has been shaped so tightly around one driver that it is hard to imagine another. One write-up on Kim's Substack said Huang has more or less admitted he does not know what happens to Nvidia after he leaves. For a company that makes up about 8% of the S&P 500, that is a real risk to millions of people's savings.
What a young founder should NOT copy

Do not copy the public humiliation unless you have his record, because most founders only have his volume. Do not copy 60 reports at a 12-person startup, since he says himself the idea doesn't scale downwards and his staff are seasoned veterans. Do not copy the sleep. Do not play down a risky revenue source to investors. __Copy the honesty with Sega, the patience with CUDA and the discipline of the first hour.__ Those were free, and they are what actually saved him.

Jensen Huang is 63 and has been president, CEO and a director of Nvidia for every day of its existence since 1993. He sits on no other public company board. He told reporters in January 2026 how he has lasted that long: “The secret for being CEO for this long is 1, don't get fired, and 2, don't get bored.”
The money

On 2 October 2026 Forbes put him at ==$204.5 billion==, the seventh-richest person in the world, after Nvidia shares hit a record. Six days later he was back below $200 billion, after a report on OpenAI's revenue knocked tech stocks and Nvidia closed at $230.48. Those swings tell you how his wealth really works. It is almost entirely Nvidia shares, valued by outsiders, and estimates vary between trackers.

For example: Nvidia's 2026 proxy lists 870,604,104 shares against Huang's name. At $230.48 a share, that block is worth about $200.7 billion on paper. Every $1 the stock moves changes its value by about $870 million, so one bad afternoon can erase more than most founders will ever earn.
The company

On 26 August 2026 Nvidia reported ==$96.2 billion== in quarterly revenue, up 106% in a year, and forecast about $108 billion for the next quarter. Finance chief Colette Kress told analysts to expect about 70% growth in the following fiscal year, and said supply was the limit. Huang's message was that AI had turned from promise to profit. It is a long way from having one month of payroll in the bank.
AI has reached its inflection point. It's doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang, Nvidia earnings statement, 26 August 2026

blocks.text: A company he started at a Denny's now forecasts $108 billion a quarter.
The bets

He answered the question about the next gamble back in 2023, in one word: Omniverse, Nvidia's simulated version of the real world. It now sits underneath what he calls physical AI, or AI that acts in the real world through robots, factories and cars. At GTC Berlin on 21 October 2026, he put humanoid robots and self-driving at the centre, with a reference robot built with Germany's Agile Robots due in early 2027. He even spent part of the keynote talking to small robot ducks.

He is also trying to widen Nvidia's grip beyond chips. In September 2026 it agreed to buy the AI model hub Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, in a deal expected to close in 2027. In Berlin he showed seven Vera Rubin racks packed into a shipping container, to bring computing online faster. Nvidia has lined up partners to mobilise more than $500 billion of outside capital for AI building. He has said he hopes Nvidia will someday be a 50,000-employee company with 100 million AI assistants.

Says the $100 billion OpenAI plan was “never a commitment”; skips the India AI Impact Summit.

Reports $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue with Vera Rubin in full production.
Agrees to buy Hugging Face; the DOJ's Groq inquiry is reported.
Tours Europe and Kazakhstan; GTC Berlin; neocloud shares slump; investor suit reaches a deal.

blocks.text: The worries

The risks are bigger than the old ones. Nvidia now acts as banker to part of its own customer base, and CNBC called the October selloff in cloud companies its first big stress test. Huang admitted capital itself is getting tight: “The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital,” he said, adding, “That's going to get solved.” A forecast with zero China compute revenue is a real wound. His own stretch pay targets for fiscal 2026 were automatically lowered because of export limits, though Nvidia's $215.9 billion in revenue beat even the original $190 billion goal.
Peak success, and he says he feels exactly as scared. Believe him.
What he says he wants next

Ask what he wants next and he talks about work, not retirement. On a week-and-a-half European tour in October 2026 he met UK, French and German leaders, and then he went to Kazakhstan to pitch it as an AI hub. He says his job is to create the conditions for people to do their life's work, and he appears to mean his own too. In January he said he would stay “for as long as I deserve it”, and he has earlier floated another 30 to 40 years.
We are the captain of this industry and we have supply chain partners and collaboration partners all over the world who are counting on us to do our part.
blocks.who: Jensen Huang at CES, reported by Quartz, January 2026

blocks.text: So picture him now. He is a 63-year-old in a leather jacket, up early reading five-bullet emails from a company worth trillions, and still using a line he first used when the bank account was nearly empty. Witt thinks that if you gave him a full day off, he would most likely start another business. __The boy who says he was the best bathroom cleaner the world has ever seen is still trying to be the best at the job in front of him.__

lessons.title: Do your most important work first.
lessons.text: Huang starts each morning with the top item on his priority list, before he even gets to the office. By the time people start interrupting him, his day is already a success. You can copy this tomorrow, and it costs nothing.

lessons.title: Tell the bad news early.
lessons.text: When Huang realised Nvidia's Sega chip was wrong, he told Sega's boss to find another partner and asked to be paid anyway. Sega agreed, and that gave Nvidia six months to live. Hiding the problem would have killed the company.

lessons.title: Stay a little afraid.
lessons.text: For more than 30 years Huang has told staff that Nvidia is 30 days from going out of business, and he says the feeling has never left him. Fear keeps you looking around corners when success tells you to relax. Just don't let it run your whole life, because he admits it is exhausting.

lessons.title: Lower your expectations and raise your effort.
lessons.text: He told Stanford students that high expectations produce low resilience, and wished them ample pain and suffering. He had already cleaned bathrooms at nine, so nothing later felt beneath him. Expect it to be hard, then be pleasantly surprised.

lessons.title: No job is beneath you.
lessons.text: “You can't show me a task that's beneath me,” he told Stanford's business students, and his proof was the toilets he cleaned as a boy. At 15 he washed dishes at Denny's and treated it like a craft. Founders who won't do the small jobs rarely get to the big ones.

lessons.title: Build where nobody is standing.
lessons.text: He put CUDA into every chip in 2007 while shareholders complained and the market cap hovered just above a billion dollars. Years later, researchers came and the AI boom ran on it. If a market already has a size on a slide, you are probably late.

lessons.title: Know what you will walk away from.
lessons.text: Nvidia left the phone chip market even though it was huge, because it wasn't where Nvidia could make a unique contribution. That retreat freed it to build for robots and cars. Choosing what to give up is a decision, not a defeat.

lessons.title: Don't let your information rot on its way up.
lessons.text: He relies on Top-5 emails because status reports get cleaned of bad news at every layer. Reading them daily, he picked up weak signals such as early interest in machine learning. Even in a five-person team, make it easy to hear the uncomfortable truth directly.

lessons.title: Share information instead of hoarding it.
lessons.text: He runs 60-plus direct reports with almost no private meetings, so everyone hears the same reasoning at the same time. He says power should come from your ability to reason and help others, not from what you know that others don't. Start this while your team is small, when it is easiest.

lessons.title: Reason out loud.
lessons.text: At Nvidia he works through problems in front of the group, and he admits that half the time he is the one who's wrong. That teaches people how to think, not only what to do. Do it, but keep his honesty and skip his temper.

lessons.title: Be honest with investors about your risky revenue.
lessons.text: “Crypto is small for us” led to a $5.5 million SEC penalty and an investor suit that ran for nearly eight years and reached the Supreme Court. Nvidia never admitted wrongdoing, but the distraction was enormous. When a hot, shaky revenue source shows up, say so loudly and early.

lessons.title: Being great doesn't mean everyone will trust you.
lessons.text: The Arm deal looked brilliant to Huang, but customers and regulators feared giving Nvidia that much control, and Nvidia took a $1.36 billion charge when it collapsed. Before a big move, ask who gets hurt if it works. Those people will be the ones who stop you.

lessons.title: Don't mistake cruelty for standards.
lessons.text: Staff call his worst outbursts the Wrath of Huang, and some still stay because they know he believes in them and rarely fires anyone. That loyalty took decades and a lot of wealth to earn, and you have neither yet. Be demanding about the work and careful with the person.

lessons.title: Find your craft and stop rushing.
lessons.text: A gardener in Kyoto, picking dead moss with bamboo tweezers, told Huang, “I have cared for my garden for 25 years. I have plenty of time.” Huang has now spent 33 years on one company. Pick a craft worth that, and speed will stop feeling like panic.

lessons.title: Choose people who will not give up on you.
lessons.text: Asked how he survived the emotional damage of building Nvidia, Huang named his family and the colleagues who have stayed for 30 years. He also says that knowing all the pain in advance, he wouldn't start again. Do not start this journey alone.

factCheck.method: Huang's own words were taken from primary transcripts wherever possible: Stripe's official transcript and its YouTube version, Stanford GSB, Acquired, CBS 60 Minutes, NVIDIA's blog, and Nvidia's earnings release. Legal and financial outcomes come from the SEC press release, SEC filings (8-K, proxy, 10-K note), court orders (Ninth Circuit in the GPU litigation, the N.D. Cal. orders in the securities and Nazemian cases) and established press. Workplace accounts from former staff come from the on-the-record excerpt of Tae Kim's book on Marketplace, the New Yorker, and Bloomberg's report, whose sources were anonymous and are labelled so. Witt's book was used only through reputable reviews and interviews (Telegraph, Atlantic, NYT, Business Insider, Taipei Times/CNA, The Conversation). Most pages were read in full. The WSJ, the NYT tax story, Bloomberg's pay and Groq stories, Bloomberg Law, both Law360 items and the Reuters items were read in part or through preview text and search excerpts, so only what those excerpts state is used. Forum posts, LinkedIn posts, podcast notes and an unauthorised book copy that surfaced in search were treated as leads only and are not cited.

disputed.note: He has given different answers at different times: 4 a.m. to exercise and see family (FT 2020, via CNBC), 5 a.m. with bed by 9:30 p.m. (Norges 2023), 6 a.m. because of his dogs (Stripe 2024), and checking email from 4 a.m. (Rogan 2025, via Fortune). The chapter presents these as a changing answer, not one fact.

disputed.claim: How many direct reports he has
disputed.note: Huang and the press have given 40, 50, 55 and 60-plus across 2023 to 2026. A search summary also gave 36, attributed to an internal list seen by Business Insider, but we could not find that report, so it is not used. We use 60-plus, his own number in 2026.
Huang says seven days a week. The Conversation's review of Witt's book says over 12 hours a day, six days a week. We use Huang's own statement.

disputed.claim: How long T5T emails have existed and how many he reads
disputed.note: The WSJ says decades; the Telegraph's review says all staff have emailed lists since 2020. Reads are put at about 100 a morning (WSJ, 2023 Sana interview) or hundreds (Tae Kim). Huang separately told Rogan he reads several thousand emails of all kinds a day. We attribute each number.

disputed.claim: Venue of the March 2024 'pain and suffering' remarks
disputed.note: CNBC places them at Stanford's SIEPR event; Fortune describes them as part of a Stanford GSB interview. We say only 'Stanford'.

disputed.claim: Price of the failed Arm deal
disputed.note: Announced at $40 billion. The rising Nvidia share price later pushed reported value to about $60 billion (NYT), $66 billion (The Register) or up to $80 billion (Reuters). We use the announced figure and note it was 'then valued'.

disputed.claim: Size of the Groq licensing deal
disputed.note: Reuters, citing the NYT, says $17 billion; Bloomberg says $20 billion. The chapter gives no figure and calls the DOJ inquiry reported, as neither Nvidia nor the DOJ has confirmed its scope.

The 2026 proxy lists 3.58% beneficial ownership; Bloomberg's index says about 3.4%; Forbes says roughly 3%. Definitions differ, for example over family trusts and foundation shares. Proxy figure used, worded as 'listed against his name'.
Huang says 95% fell to zero. Other estimates differ: a September 2026 analysis cited IDC at about 55% of AI accelerator cards shipped in China in 2025. His figure is quoted as his own statement.

disputed.claim: Outcome of the crypto investor suit
disputed.note: Law360 reported on 23 October 2026 that investors told the judge a deal had been reached. We could read only the summary, so the amount, terms and court approval are unconfirmed as of 2 November 2026.
Witt reports that some staff see Huang's outbursts as deliberate theatre, and former staff told Bloomberg of real fights and shouting. Both are presented; neither is stated as the final truth.
